Mr. Speaker, the shortness of this debate on second reading indicates that this bill has commended itself pretty well to the house. When the resolution was before the committee on February 28 last I gave an outline of its main points. As the hon. member for Hamilton West pointed out, this bill provides that compensation shall be at the rate effective in the province in which the injured person is normally employed rather than the province in which the injury takes place. Second, it includes persons in government employ not paid by direct wage or salary. Third, employees assigned to foreign posts are covered for compensation purposes by the Ontario rate. Fourth, the act will recognize locally engaged employees in Canadian offices abroad.
The reason I recapitulate these four points is that there is a fifth that I did not touch on very fully, and that was an oversight. That is a change that has to do with third party cases. In the past an employee injured while on duty by an outside party or disabled through defective conditions in buildings or for other causes had the choice of taking the compensation under the act and surrendering claim for damages against the crown or, on the other hand, of taking legal action himself for an amount which he felt would adequately compensate him. If he collected less than he would have received for medical care and compensation under the act, the difference was payable to him. If he obtained a greater judgment than the value of the benefits under the act, he was that much better off.
On the other hand, if he decided to take the benefits provided under the act the crown was subrogated to his rights of redress against the third party. There would be action in the name of Her Majesty, and if there happened to be a judgment for an amount greater than the cost of hospital, medical care and compensation, the excess would be paid into the consolidated revenue fund.
The change here will permit payment of any excess judgment money to the employee, subject to the government being relieved up
	t

to the amount of the excess for further treatment or compensation in connection with the same injury. Usually, however, the crown suit has been for the actual amount paid out under the compensation act; therefore there was no excess to worry about.
Also, in the past there has had to be a court judgment before the employee could be paid the difference between the judgment and the cost of medical care and value of compensation. In future he can receive this difference if the Minister of Labour approves of a compromise after out of court settlement. I thought I would give that explanation of the fifth point to have it on the record.
The object of this bill, of course, is to do in this field of workmen's compensation what the government is doing or trying to do in all other of its relations with its employees, namely to make possible conditions of public service as beneficial to the employee as is provided by good private employers. With that yardstick we are perhaps justified in retaining the association with the provincial compensation boards rather than setting up full federal machinery, as I think was hinted at by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni this afternoon. I would remind the house, too, that such a federal board would be very expensive to administer when it is considered that the federal employees to be served are scattered throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and some of them beyond the shores of Canada.
The hon. member for Hamilton West referred to the travelling federal worker. Of course, even if he were travelling all the time and carried his office in his pockets he would have some federal government office to which he would report, and the province in which that office was located would be the province which would provide his workmen's compensation. For instance, I can visualize a federal employee in the city of Montreal doing a great deal of travelling in the Atlantic provinces. In that case his injuries would be taken care of by the workmen's compensation laws of the province of Quebec.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to university students employed by federal government departments during the summer months. I would point out that the laws of compensation in all provinces have limitations, which I might paraphrase in this way. An accident or an illness suffered must be related to the regular duties of the employee if he or she is to qualify for benefits. Under that limitation, of course, if an employee, whether temporary or permanent, is injured or contracts a disease that is not related to his regular work, he does not

qualify under any workmen's compensation act. But if the university student working in the summer is injured in the course of his duties it would be possible for him to make application for benefits under this legislation in exactly the same way as though he were a permanent civil servant.

Now that hon. members have had a chance to study the bill it may be seen that it contains only a few amendments to sections, and that generally speaking they are designed to assist in the administration of the act and to remove a few inconsistencies that in the first year of operating the act have become apparent.
As I indicated the other day in speaking on the resolution, the principal amendment deals with the extension for a limited period the time within which new contributors to the superannuation account may elect to contribute for prior service. This is necessitated because of the tremendous influx of contributors under this new act in 1954, nearly all of whom have periods of prior service for which they wish to elect.
The amendments will also make it possible to revoke or alter an election by reducing the remaining instalments to be paid and thereby reducing the entitlement to pension. I shall explain this later when we come to deal with the sections of the bill. The terms and conditions under which this would be permitted are proposed to be left to the governor in council, but I may say that the intention would be to apply this provision particularly in cases of real financial difficulty occurring after the election is made, or if perchance the estimated cost of the election 50433-1411
Public Service Superannuation Act was calculated on the basis of incorrect information, as is found to be the case from time to time.
The only major extension in coverage under the amendments will be to include sessional employees of the Senate and the House of Commons as contributors upon designation by the governor in council, as is already being done in the case of prevailing rate and seasonal employees. Apart from this there are one or two other minor extensions in coverage which I shall be prepared to explain when we are discussing the individual sections of the bill.
The other amendments deal with certain aspects of the transfer provisions when a person moves from a position under the Defence Services Pension Act or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act to one under the Public Service Superannuation Act, and with some purely administrative points. There are one or two minor inconsistencies in the benefit provisions which have become apparent during the first year of operation of the act. All of these are of a minor nature and in these cases also I shall be prepared to give an explanation when the individual clauses are before the committee.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: In so far as the sessional people are concerned, and in so far as their prior service in concerned, it is a voluntary thing. This amount is in the estimates once a year and put before parliament.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Referring to what the hon. member for Fort William said, if an employee has had over 10 or 20 years' service and makes arrangements with the Department of Finance to pay for that service, then the government automatically matches that payment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Matches the employee's contribution annually.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: If these sessional employees have not paid in anything, will they get anything?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. If they become contributors then the government will match their contribution and from then on they become entitled to the regular provisions of the act.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I am referring to the question asked by my colleague the hon. member for Perth. If the parliamentary assistant is not informed, I am sure the hon. member for Perth is not asking these questions out of idle curiosity, and if he feels he needs that information might it not be made available?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I would have no hesitation in assisting the hon. member by consultation with Mr. Speaker to see if that information could not be obtained. I have no doubt it could. When a decision of this kind is reached it does not affect the ways and means immediately, because such moneys as will be required from parliament in matching grants will not be in this year's estimates.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I believe the hon. member for Greenwood intimated that there were some 12,000 employees still not under the Public Service Superannuation Act. He also intimated that in his estimation the majority of those would now be coming under the act; is that correct?

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: People who will not come under the act until this bill is passed are sessional employees, such as we have been discussing here. There are also persons here and elsewhere who are on a part-time basis, or persons who have been engaged for work that is not considered to be of more than 12 months' duration. Every year there are new employees who, on the anniversary of entering the service, do become contributors. There will always be, in a staff as large as that of the government, a certain number who are on part-time or on a prevailing rate and have not accumulated adequate service, or are sessional employees who have not had 60 months of service and so on, who will not be under the act.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: That would include the workers on canals who are only employed for five or six months?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: That is right; they would be part-time. They might be seasonal employees.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: May I revert to a question I asked once before? Is there any starting age in the act that would have any bearing on the position of the page boys? subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: It would only count, Mr. Chairman, if the original work was classified as full-time work. They would be disqualified under the definition of temporary employee if it were only part-time work. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Who decides what is a full day's work for page boys? It seems to me that they put in a pretty full day.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: That interests me, and I just ask this question for information. Let us take, for example, the postal employees across Canada. subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: No, temporary.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION

speechtext: I am just wondering if paragraph (d) of this clause means that there were some employees receiving over $600 and below $900 per year who had been refused participation in the fund. They were cut off as at January 1, 1954, and are now being reinstated; is that it?

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Yes. I could give an explanation of that. Under the former act the lowest salary limit for contributors was $600. Under the present act this limit was raised to $900, and that was done on the understanding that no full-time employee would be dropped as a contributor. It turns out, however, that a number of lightkeepers in Newfoundland earning salaries under $900 were unintentionally dropped. The amendment will have the effect of bringing those employees back under the act.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I am wondering what special circumstances require this change in the act. I note the addition of the words "except under such circumstances", and so on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
I mentioned that sometimes an employee in the public service will elect to contribute for prior service, and will do so on the basis of some incorrect calculation. It might be a non-professional calculation as to the amount he would be called upon to pay to discharge his part of the bargain he has elected to enter into.
The act at the moment is so rigid that even if it was found later by the actuaries in the superannuation branch that he had been misinformed and had undertaken to do more than he feels he should do, nevertheless he is unable to withdraw from that election. The result would be that he would come to the age of retirement and might not have paid the amount he elected to pay. There would probably then be some interval of time after the time of retirement, when he would draw nothing because his annuity would be assigned in payment of the debt in accordance with his original election.
There is no desire to relieve people unduly, or to allow them to withdraw from the superannuation scheme at a time when they are likely to need it. But there are instances of hardship such as I have described, and it is felt that the act is too rigid and that some discretion should be permitted.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
The clause as it was contained a definite statement as to the rights of the elector. Then there is an addition which is put in general terms;
-except under such circumstances and upon such terms and conditions, including payment by the elector to Her Majesty of such amount in respect of any benefit accruing ... as the governor in council by regulation prescribes.
Does this mean there will be an attempt to make regulations covering a situation which is not covered by the clause as it stands? In other words does it mean there

Public Service Superannuation Act will be a known situation which any civil servant can discover, that steps will be taken to make regulations, and that it will not be a matter of their having to be taken up when applications are made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: No. There are broad regulations now known to everybody in the service, and these have stemmed from the basic act. There are a number of things the act itself says are to be governed by regulation. There is an order in council available to all, and the broad terms to describe what constitutes hardship will doubtless be made known in a regulation of that kind.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-Woman deemed to be widow.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: It seems to me that clauses 6 and 7 go together. Apparently there are certain persons who have been prohibited in the past from receiving benefits. This measure would change that in the future, it would seem, so far as persons in that situation are concerned. Will it affect those who have been refused the same consideration in the past?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Yes. The essence of this is that, as in the veterans Pension Act, there is provision for paying a pension to what is described as a common law wife of a retired civil servant. Through inadvertence the act as now drawn provides that if those two people become free to marry after the person who was pensioned had retired, and do marry, she would be disentitled in respect of pension, although if they remained unmarried the pension would have continued in accordance with our regulations. It is to correct that situation. If otherwise entitled, marriage to the contributor after the time of retirement would not disentitle the woman.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Is it retroactive to January 1, 1954?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Yes. Then with respect to clause 7, this again is something that has come to light. If there was a second marriage after retirement the children of the first marriage born before retirement are cut off under the terms of the act as presently drafted. To correct that situation this amendment is required.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 7 agreed to.
On clause 8-Persons re-employed.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Would the minister give a word of explanation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Certain older contributors have periods of free pensionable service. This


is as a result of legislation which existed for the period 1924 to 1927, and also certain other privileges available up to 1939. It is possible that such a person might leave the service and then become re-employed in the public service. As the act now stands such a person would lose the free service that was available to him under this earlier legislation. The amendment is to correct that situation.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 9-Medical examination requirements.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: This change indicates that an election to pay for any prior service is void unless medical examination is undergone. The old section reads that a contributor is not entitled to elect to pay for any prior service unless medical examination is undergone. I wonder what type of case woulcf arise to cause this change?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: There is no change in the type of case that would demand prior medical examination before becoming a contributor under the scheme. But it is required, as the act is now worded, that medical examination take place within 30 days before the election.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Is that according to the regulations?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: No, it is in the act, and again it is found to be too restrictive. It is possible that under certain circumstances a reasonable period of time would be required after election in which to have the medical and within which the government may accept the election.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 10-Election by unestablished Newfoundland civil servant.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: This would seem to be a desirable clause, and I support it. I note its purpose is to bring under the provisions of the Public Service Superannuation Act those employees in Newfoundland who were known as unestablished civil servants.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Similar to our old temporaries.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
The parliamentary assistant is trying to get ahead of me. I was going to suggest that this category would be similar to the old department of soldiers' civil re-establishment. They were unestablished. They were in a department that had not been recognized as a department of government. As l read the language of the section it seems to me that the cases are not dissimilar. My suggestion is the obvious one. If it is possible to do this for this group we should

be able to accord the privilege of transferring to part II of the Public Service Superannuation Act to that other group of employees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I fail to see that analogy, and I repeat it is felt that as the functions that were formerly performed by the province of Newfoundland are now federal functions, and since we have made certain changes in the privileges of temporary employees who are similar to the unestablished civil servant designation formerly in effect in Newfoundland, we should permit those employees to have exactly the same advantage as they would have had if they had stayed on in the service of the government of Newfoundland and had become established civil servants in the province of Newfoundland. If they had become established, passing on from the grade of unestablished, they would have been entitled to elect for half of their previous years of service, and that is what is proposed here.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
There is one point I am not quite sure of. I refer to paragraph (9) of section 10, which reads:
For the purposes of this act, the salary deemed to have been received by a contributor to whom subsection (8) applies, during any period of service described in that subsection, is a salary at the initial rate authorized to be paid to him upon ' becoming employed in the public service.
I do not quite understand it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: What is involved here, of course, is payment for prior service. The salary upon which the contributions will be paid will be the salary that employee became entitled to when he entered the service of Canada, having left the service of Newfoundland.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 11-Service countable.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
I should like to say just a few words with respect to clause 11. As I read it I confess it seems rather technical and involved, but I believe it is one of the clauses referred to by the parliamentary assistant as designed to iron out some of the difficulties where employees transfer from one service to another. In this case the relationship seems to be between service in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and service in some department of government covered by the Public Service Superannuation Act.
I welcome most heartily any and all of these moves that are made to increase what I sometimes call the mobility or the transferability of pension rights. I think it is one of the most important problems in the whole field of pensions in our country at the present time. A great many people are denied access 50433-142J
21, 1955	2239
Public Service Superannuation Act to certain employment because they are too old to qualify for pension rights in that field of employment. Others are frozen in their present employment because they cannot move elsewhere without losing such pension rights as they have built up to that point.
It does seem to me that we should move as rapidly as we can to the position' where people can move from public service to private service and from private service to public service, or from one field to another, and carry with them their pension rights and benefits. Of course that could be expedited to a certain extent by the Minister of Finance if we had a certain fiscal policy that would permit that sort of thing. But sooner or later it is going to call for more than that. It is going to call for some master plan under the sponsorship of the government if we are to have full mobility and transferability of pension rights. I can think of individuals who come to my mind, people in one type of employment who go to another and who suffer quite a loss in terms of pension rights, which really is not fair.
This is not a criticism of the clause that is before us, because if I understand it, the clause does iron out some little difficulties for a restricted group in this field.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Each of the amendments makes it a little easier to do that which my hon. friend advocates in a broader way.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: The government should bring in a great many more amendments of this kind until we have in Canada complete transferability of pension rights.

On clause 12-Regulations.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Will the parliamentary
assistant tell us whether, under paragraph (d), there are many instances of this kind, and under paragraph (ga), what type of case is contemplated?

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:

Public Service Superannuation Act

speechtext: Take the young man who has been ill, is on leave of absence and keeps his payments up. Will he be all right?

speechtext: Yes.

On clause 13-Extension of time fixed for making elections in certain cases.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Apparently this is one of the main clauses in the bill as far as the parliamentary assistant is concerned. In moving the resolution he mentioned that there are some 60,000 additional contributors. How many have been processed up to December 31, 1954?

speechtext: Am I right in supposing that this can be renewed one year at a time? If the making of an election takes place on December 31, 1957, does that mean the time can actually be extended to December 31, 1958?

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise one question which I suggest is of some importance. I shall read the clause:
The governor in council may make regulations providing for the extension, under such circumstances and upon such terms and conditions as are specified in those regulations, but in no case for a period of more than one year, . . .
[DOT]-and so on. Why is the one-year limit necessary? It is not a role I like, to suggest that the government should take more power; but is it really necessary to make an arbitrary cut-off of that kind, where you might find some case that is absolutely compelling on its merits but it comes in a day late? Is it really necessary to make that cut-off? If it has to be made, while a year seems a long time in one way, in another way it may be a very short time, and I do suggest most earnestly that unless it has been seriously considered and the objections to it are quite overwhelming, the parliamentary assistant should have another look at it.	,

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
remember that in other sections of the act there are provisions for late election upon paying an interest penalty. I think most of the cases the hon. member has in mind would

be covered by that provision. The hon. member will realize that the longer you leave the door open the greater is the procrastination.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
I will admit what the
parliamentary assistant has said, but it seems to me that he has gone part of the way when he says that in certain cases the door is left partly open, with a penalty. subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Is the parliamentary
assistant saying now that there is really no final cut-off but that by the payment of penalties, etc., there is still a way of escape, that one can come in through the side door? If the parliamentary assistant is saying that, then I have nothing more to say.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I shall not press the matter further now, except to ask the parliamentary assistant to satisfy himself absolutely before third reading that that is the situation. Incidentally, I suggest that if it is, then these words should go out because if the situation is as indicated then I submit that on the face of it there is a contradiction in the bill. Without spending more time on it, I ask the parliamentary assistant to have a look at it and make a statement on third reading.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I will. Of course I do not think there is a contradiction, because within a period of a year there is no penalty.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT
subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS AND CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I am quite ready to be shown that I am wrong.

Bill reported.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES, SIGNED SEPTEMBER 10, 1954
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is one more of a series of international treaties respecting' our great fisheries. The previous treaties have been extremely successful, and we are hoping that this one will be equally so. As most hon. members know, Canada has been blessed with great fisheries both in our coastal waters and in our inland waters. Over the last 50 years we have done a pretty good job of conserving these fisheries in our own waters. I think the best proof of that is the fact that in recent years our fisheries have* been generally increasing in total size of catch, whereas many other nations have experienced declining catches.
However, we have no control over fishing activities beyond our territorial waters when that fishing is conducted by the nationals of other nations. It is an important problem for all the fishing nations of the world, because there is not much sense in having good conservation of your own fisheries if other nationals can come right up to your boundaries and exploit those stocks. Some nations of the world have recently tried to solve this problem by arbitrarily pushing out their territorial waters 10, 12, 50 or even 200 miles in an endeavour to conserve these fisheries for the sole use of their own nationals. This of course has brought immediate protests and reprisals and court actions from the nations whose fishermen have been displaced by this action. Our nation has tried a different approach to fisheries conservation on the high seas, and I think the record shows that this approach is the more successful one.
It was first tried in 1923 in the north Pacific by the United States and ourselves. The greatest halibut fishery in the world is off the Queen Charlotte islands. Ruthless fishing by the fleets of both nations had brought this great fishery to a point where it looked as though it would soon be extinct. In 1923 these two nations got together and agreed to international conservation and control, each country controlling the activities of its own nationals in those high seas waters. Here again the best proof of how successful this form of conservation has been is the record. In 1923 these fisheries were at their all-time low; last year we caught 71 million pounds of halibut, the greatest catch in all our history, in just two months of fishing. The other
Great Lakes Fisheries
pleasing thing about this is the change in Canada's share. In 1923 we got only 17 per cent of the catch; last year we got 40 per cent.
That example was followed in our second international treaty, to conserve the sockeye salmon on the west coast. Here again was a valuable fishery which was diminishing each year, and here again the record shows how successful this method of international conservation has been. Last year salmon fishing on the Fraser had the greatest catch since 1913. Almost 12 million fish went into the Adams river, just one of the branches of the Fraser, and the total catch came close to $40 million.
We also have the north Pacific fur seal convention with the United States, which has been almost too successful. Pelagic sealing for these fur seals had reduced them to about 150,000. The United States and ourselves agreed to a policy of strict control and conservation, and as a result we now have between 2 and 3 million of these animals, from which the government of Canada nets a clear profit of about $1 million a year. There are now so many seals in these waters that the United States fishermen and our own fishermen are complaining that the seals are getting more fish than they are. This fall we intend to have a meeting to study our scientists' reports and see whether or not this herd should now be reduced.
After the war, in 1946, the 17 nations of the world who follow whaling were very concerned with the great decline in the stock of whales in many of the oceans of the world. They got together and formed the international whaling commission, along pretty much the same lines as our first halibut commission. The hon. member for Kamloops recently, in an effort to bolster up a very weak speech on veterans affairs, went far enough afield to attack the whaling commission and suggested that it was not of much importance. We have good whaling stocks in the north Pacific, the Beaufort sea, Hudson bay and the coast of Newfoundland.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO IMPLEMENT CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES, SIGNED SEPTEMBER 10, 1954
speechtext:
If the hon. member, who is not a fisheries member, was listening he would know that I was trying to indicate to the committee why we are so keen about this type of international conservation. It has proved very successful in the past in these fisheries I have mentioned. I think most hon. members will admit that it is a pretty logical approach to the problem, to show that we have good reason to enter into these new international fisheries agreements
2242	HOUSE OF
Great Lakes Fisheries
on the great lakes, because our other international fisheries agreements have been so successful.
Because of the successful record of these international conservation treaties on the west coast, the ten nations that fish the northwest Atlantic got together in 1951 in a similar treaty to conserve another great fishery, the Grand Banks, which despite 400 years of fishing are still the greatest fisheries in the world. In 1953 Japan, the United States and ourselves got together under still another similar treaty to conserve the great fisheries of the north Pacific, all because Canada and the United States have proved this is an intelligent and effective way to conserve our fisheries.
Now comes one more in this series of what have been such extremely successful efforts in international co-operation, this treaty to conserve fisheries on the great lakes. The fisheries on the great lakes amount to about 40 million pounds of fish a year. That may not seem to be much as compared with our total catch of about 2,000 million pounds. Nevertheless it is extremely important to our fishermen, for two reasons.
First, there is the actual value of the catch to the fishermen of the great lakes, which is somewhere between $7 and $10 million a year. Second, there is the nature of the fisheries themselves. Most of the fisheries of the world are a long way from the market, and great expense is incurred in transporting fish from where they are caught to where they are consumed. Halibut from the Queen Charlotte islands, for example, is transported almost 3,000 miles to eastern Canada or the eastern states, and lake trout from Great Slave lake 2,000 miles to Chicago and Toronto.
Here on the great lakes we have these fisheries right in the centre of the greatest concentration of population on the North American continent, a fact which makes them extremely valuable fisheries. Within recent years, however, there has been a steady decline, not so much in the volume of catch but in the value of the catch in the great lakes.
The most valuable fish commercially are the lake trout and the whitefish. There is no question that the parasite, the sea lamprey, has wreaked great havoc on the lake trout and the whitefish. Another reason is that perhaps overfishing for those valuable species has put the fishery out of balance and resulted in greater populations of the cheaper fish. Those two factors show the need for intelligent international conservation and control. It must be international because, as with the high seas, there is not much point in our


having an effective program of conservation and regulation of fishing on our side of the great lakes if there is not a similar program on the other side. Fish are no respecters of the international boundary down the centre of the great lakes and move freely back and forth.
For some years we have been trying to achieve this treaty. We have had difficulties, not through any lack of interest on the part of the United States government-because they are as much aware as we are of the success of our joint treaties on the Pacific coast and the need for a similar treaty on the great lakes-but rather because of the problem of jurisdiction. Here in Canada, of course, fisheries are the responsibility of the federal government. In the United States, however, the primary control rests with the states. There are eight states fringing the great lakes, some of them such as Ohio with very good fisheries and others with a short coast line with insignificant fisheries. It was apparently difficult to persuade all of them to surrender the necessary authority to the federal government. However, the United States government has now achieved this objective, and was able to negotiate on behalf of the states.
I am happy to report that we have ho such difficulties on this side of the border. We have had the closest co-operation from the province of Ontario. Even before this treaty was signed we had embarked with them on a joint program of research and had launched a program by ourselves of lamprey control. Last year in the estimates we had an amount of $15,000 to match $15,000 Ontario put up for research, and $150,000 for lamprey control. Now we have this new treaty to carry out international conservation on the great lakes.
Perhaps I should read the objectives which were set out. The convention provides for the establishment of a commission composed of two national sections of three members each, appointed by the contracting governments. This is the same pattern as that of the other international treaties. The principal duties of the commission are as follows:
(1)	To formulate a research program with a view of determining the need for conservation measures in respect of any stock of fish of common concern to the fisheries of Canada and the United States;
(2)	to co-ordinate research and to undertake any research by the commission where necessary;
(3)	to recommend appropriate measures to the contracting governments based on such research;

(4)	to formulate and implement a comprehensive program for the purpose of eradicating or minimizing the sea lamprey menace.
The commission has no power to make regulations. In that respect it is the same as most of the other international commissions. It has only authority to recommend any necessary measure, leaving the regulating of fishing activities to the respective governments. In other words, each of us passes the regulations recommended to control our own nationals.
The joint expenses of the commission are to be apportioned between Canada and the United States in the manner agreed to between the two governments after recommendation by the commission. The expenses of each national section are to be paid by the respective governments.
The convention covers all the great lakes and their connecting waters, and will come into force on the date of exchange of ratifications and remain in force for ten years. It may remain in effect thereafter until terminated by notice by either country.
When the bill is before the house for second reading I shall then propose to refer it to the standing committee on marine and fisheries, so that hon. members may have an opportunity to question our officials on the actual program they contemplate.
In closing I may say that with the ratification of this international commission on the great lakes we shall have only one major fishery of Canada left unprotected by such an international commission. I refer to the pink salmon fishery on the Pacific coast. For some time we have been negotiating to arrange a similar treaty with the Americans on this fishery, and I think after the fishing program we have planned for this summer we shall be able to achieve that objective during the fall.

We are happy to know that this resolution is to be referred to the committee, or that at least the minister will suggest or recommend that it be referred to the committee where we can give it careful study.
As I think the minister has pointed out, the question of jurisdiction has interfered with the proper enforcement of conservation or
Great Lakes Fisheries protective measures in the past. We cannot have eight states on one side of the line and one province on the other side of the line, with one set of provisions on the United States side and one set on this side, without having a great deal of perhaps not misunderstanding or conflict but certainly lack of co-operation. Following the passage of this legislation we shall have dealings between the two central governments; we shall have increased moneys for research, and apparently we shall have a really definite effort made to meet the menace of the lamprey eel which is threatening the existence of a valuable part of the fisheries on the great lakes.
It does not matter so much to the fishermen that their tonnage remains the same if at the same time they are catching more of the cheaper fish and fewer of the more valuable fish. That is the situation which has prevailed during the past few years. We are therefore glad this resolution is finally before the house. We hope the bill will be referred to the committee in the very near future, where it may receive further consideration and then be brought into effect as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe this measure will meet with wide approval among the men on the great lakes who, by their skill and knowledge, endeavour to make their livelihood in the fishing industry. The fishing industry, especially along the north shore of lake Erie, has its place in the economy of our country. The 1954 estimated total catch of fish for the province of Ontario amounts to some 47 million pounds. Of this total nearly two-thirds, or 30 million pounds, were caught in the waters of lake Erie. This does not mean that lake Erie fishermen are becoming wealthy in the fishing industry; far from it. Statistics show that the average income of a fisherman is less than $2,000 a year.
The problems of the great lakes fishermen are somewhat different from those of the hardy fishermen who carry on their operations mainly on our coastal waters. The spring fishing season on lake Erie opens on March 1, but very often on this date fishermen find their boats still frozen in the harbours and there is a period of several weeks when they must combat the drifting ice floes which very often do serious damage to their nets.
To bear this out, I have a clipping here from the Aylmer Express of March 17, stating that commercial fishermen from the fishing village of Port Bruce were delayed by the recent cold snap which left a layer of ice some six inches deep on the water surface. The two fishermen who have been operating out of the village for nearly three weeks so far have not brought in a single fish this season. The article goes on to say that considerable heavy ice is still visible for some distance offshore but the harbour mouth and shoreline water are perfectly clear. This will indicate to some extent one of the problems which

these fishermen have in the spring, when the price of fish is usually much higher than it is later on in the season.
In recent years the catch of fish on some of the great lakes has seriously fallen off, to a point where many species of fish are rapidly being depleted. One factor that has entered into the depletion of fish, as the minister mentioned, is the sea lamprey, more commonly known by local fishermen in my constituency as the lamprey eel. The cycle of this parasite was that it spent its early life in fresh water, migrated to the ocean where it grew to maturity, and then returned to fresh water to spawn. It was during its life in the ocean that it became a parasite on fish. Since the early twenties the cycle of this parasite has changed, and now we find the lamprey spending the entire cycle of its life in fresh water.
The first large spawning population of sea lamprey was discovered in 1932 in a tributary of lake Erie. From this area it migrated to lake Huron, where it found the shoals advantageous to spawning. In lake Huron it found the lake trout to its liking to feed upon to such an extent that today the catch of lake trout in lake Huron is practically exhausted. During the parasite phase of its life the lamprey feeds on the blood and body juices of fish. It attaches itself to its victim by means of its sucker-like mouth, and with its sharp teeth soon rasps a hole in the body of the fish. Experiments have proven that a lamprey will remain attached to the body of the fish for as long as three weeks, provided the fish does not die. The more delicate species of fish die very quickly, but the hardy species may survive one attachment or more. The attack of the lamprey has not been limited only to lake trout but has involved many other species of fish, especially white-fish.
In reviewing figures released by the Ontario department of lands and forests we find that the estimated Ontario catch of fish in all the great lakes has increased slightly in 1954 to a total of 34,513,000 pounds, an increase of 7-2 per cent over the 1953 preliminary estimate of 32,209,000 pounds. Then let us take a look at the figures for lake Huron and Georgian bay. We find that commercial landings in Georgian bay show a decrease of 38 per cent, from 4,682,000 pounds in 1953 to 2,897,000 pounds in 1954, due to a drop of 41-5 per cent in the catch of white-fish, the principal species sought. Other decreases were noted in northern inland waters where 4,300,000 pounds were taken, 10 per cent under the 1953 figure. For lake Ontario the figure was 1,212,000 pounds, down 10 per cent; for lake Huron it was 1,031,000
Great Lakes Fisheries pounds, down 8 per cent; for north channel it was 253,000 pounds, down 17 per cent, and for southern inland waters the figure was
442.000	pounds, down 19 per cent.
To show further the decrease in the catch of lake trout, especially in lake Huron, I wish to use figures from the United States department of the interior, fish and wildlife services, contained in a bulletin published in October, 1950, entitled "The Sea Lamprey in the Great Lakes". They express grave fear that this parasite may completely destroy fishing for this species.
The speed and completeness with which the lake trout fishery has collapsed in lake Huron is demonstrated by the following record of the catch in United States waters from 1935 through 1948. I do not intend to quote in full the figures for the period from 1935 to 1948, but will take a five-year period commencing with 1935. In 1935 the catch was 1,743,000 pounds, and five years later it was down to
940.000	pounds. The catch continued to decrease and by 1945 was down to 172,000 pounds. The last figures available to me were for 1948, when the catch was only 4,000 pounds. A tentative figure for 1949 was set at only 912 pounds. This production figure has set a new low record for any year since 1939. These figures illustrate, Mr. Speaker, the destruction that has taken place in one of our great lakes as a result, in a great measure, of the attack of the sea lamprey on the great lakes fish.
Another problem which confronts the fishing industry, especially in lake Erie, is the natural mortality of the fish. In some species natural mortality follows spawning, but many people are of the opinion that a fish continues to grow larger as the years go by. This is not the case. A fish has a life span just as any other animal has.
I have already mentioned the problem of parasites, in addition to which there is the problem of disease, and this is also a matter of international concern. Another cause for the depletion of the fish is the high temperature of the water in the summer, added to which we have the old difficulty of the pollution of international rivers and streams. Pollution has become quite a problem in recent years, especially in those waters bordering southwestern Ontario and along lake Ontario. No doubt this problem of pollution will increase as industry continues to grow in this greatly expanding area bordering along the great lakes in this part of Ontario.
When implemented this resolution should meet with the approval of all fishermen on the inland lakes. We hope it will enable Canada and the United States to jointly carry on research work, not only in an
2246	HOUSE OF
Great Lakes Fisheries
endeavour to eradicate the sea lamprey but also with the aim of restocking our lakes. I know there are many other problems which confront our fishermen on these inland lakes, but we do hope this convention that will establish the great lakes fisheries commission will prove of great benefit to all those fishermen who make their living in these waters.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 259, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: I shall be very brief, Mr. Speaker. At the resolution stage I outlined the recommendations of the board of transport commissioners as contained in the grade crossing report, and indicated the main lines of the legislation which the government proposed to introduce. Hon. members have now had an opportunity to study the actual wording in the bill and the explanatory notes. Perhaps it would be helpful, however, if I were to compare the present provisions of the act with the proposed amendments.
1.	At present the fund may be applied only in respect of actual construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public at existing crossings at rail level. It cannot be applied toward the cost of repairing or improving existing subways, bridges or other grade separations. The proposed legislation would make the fund available to aid the reconstruction and improvement of grade separations which are obsolete for highway traffic using them, the construction in any one case not to exceed 30 per cent of the cost nor $150,000 per project.
2.	Under existing legislation no contribution from the fund may be made toward newly opened crossing protection unless existing crossings are closed. The proposed legislation would empower the board to make contributions where it sees fit toward the cost of grade separations in any location, provided that existing crossings are closed or nearly all the highway traffic using existing crossings is to be diverted to the new crossing.

3.	At present the fund cannot be applied to the protection of crossings constructed after April 1, 1909, unless an approved agreement has been concluded between the railway and other parties bearing a portion of the cost of the work. The proposed legislation eliminates this provision, except that the crossing must have been in existence for at least three years prior to the board's order authorizing a grant from the fund.
4.	Whereas the maximum grant for any one crossing is now 40 per cent of the cost with a maximum of $150,000 per project, it is proposed that the maximum grant be increased to 60 per cent of the cost with a maximum of $300,000 per project.
5.	Whereas the present appropriation to the fund is $1 million annually, it is proposed that the annual appropriation be $5 million, with a proviso that where on April 1 in any year there is an uncommitted balance of more than $2 million in the fund the appropriation for that year would be such amount as with the uncommitted balance would total $7 million.
6.	The present legislation provides that where a railway is constructed across a highway after May, 1909, the railway shall bear the whole cost of protection unless an approved agreement has been concluded between the railway and other parties bearing a portion of the cost of the work. This section would be repealed.
Perhaps I should add that after second reading of the bill it would be my intention to move that it be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was about to suggest what the minister has just said, that this matter should be referred to the committee. I do not see any great objection to what has been outlined this evening by the Minister of Transport. However, there were some features he touched upon which I believe are worthy of consideration. He pointed out that the board did not consider any grade crossing application unless the application was made by the other contracting parties, the provinces, the municipalities and the railways.
After examining the minister's remarks I am not satisfied as to the board's intention in connection with the administration of the act. I would like to have some further information, but as the hour is getting late perhaps I should not speak at greater length now. However, if it is the wish of hon. members I am prepared to continue for a while longer.
Railway Act
On Friday evening the minister intimated that there was some misapprehension as to the purpose for which the fund was created, and I was not quite clear as to his meaning when he made that statement. There has been a change made in the ratio of payments to be made on grade crossing projects. The share of the municipalities is set at 25 per cent, which is a 5 per cent reduction. However, the railway companies have received a much better break, no doubt owing to the fact that they cannot meet the necessary obligations in connection with grade crossing projects. Notwithstanding the improvement made in the ratio of contributions, I do not think this fund will accomplish what the people of Canada have in mind. I believe the board must adjust its thinking to the requirements of the people in the matter of level crossings.
In my view this is not a matter simply of spending money, but rather one of reducing the hazard; and I do not believe the thinking by the board is adjusted to that fact. The object they seem to have in mind is that of saving money. As a result the railways are not interested in removing hazards at grade crossings because the expense is so great.
Therefore in municipalities, where the cost of separating grade crossings is too great for them to bear, I believe the initiative should come from the grade crossing fund. The municipalities will not make application for those crossings because of a lack of funds. When this matter comes before the railway committee it should be considered thoroughly, and we should have before us some members of the board of transport commissioners who would be prepared to give us more information on the subject than we have at the moment. I cannot conceive of the board not having information as to how many applications have been made for railway grade crossings from one end of Canada to the other. I am sure there are plenty of applications taken at the initiative of the railways and the municipalities, and the board should be prepared to supply that information.
I believe I would not be far wrong if I were to say that there are before the board at the present time more applications than they can look after, even with the $5 million now recommended. The consensus in the house on all sides, irrespective of party, is that there is not enough money in the fund. The board has taken the attitude of seeing how tight they can hold the purse strings, with the result that no grade crossing application is considered until such time as there have been so many accidents that the situation has become serious in the public mind.

Business of the House
The suggestion that we discuss this matter in the railway committee is a good one, but I still say the minister should give careful consideration to placing enough money m the fund to take care of the requirements.
I would ask to call it ten o'clock.
On motion of Mr. Small the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we will take all third readings available, and then resume the adjourned debate on the motion to go into supply.
Then I believe I should say at this time that it is the intention to move on Thursday in such a manner that we may have the external affairs debate. I should, however, point out that the motion we have been using, namely one to refer the estimates of the Department of External Affairs to the standing committee on external affairs, is not debatable; and it will have to be understood that it is by unanimous consent that we are having the debate in this manner.
I think I also ought to ask opposition members for their co-operation in dealing with supplementary estimates on Friday, and also a motion for interim supply.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, March 22, 1955
